props.title: French Kiss
props.initialSlug: Woman chases fiancé to Paris, finds unexpected love

sections.content: French Kiss stands as a charming entry in the 90s romantic comedy boom, pairing Meg Ryan's neurotic American teacher with Kevin Kline's roguish French thief. The film cleverly subverts the typical "American in Paris" trope by having much of the action take place in the French countryside, particularly the sun-drenched vineyards of Southern France. It follows similar fish-out-of-water romantic European adventures like Only You (1994) and A Room with a View (1985), but adds a distinctly French flavor through Kline's character's obsession with wine cultivation and his scene-stealing accent work.

sections.content: The film sits comfortably within director Lawrence Kasdan's repertoire, though it's lighter fare compared to his earlier works like The Big Chill (1983) and Body Heat (1981). Ryan continues her reign as America's sweetheart following hits like When Harry Met Sally (1989) and Sleepless in Seattle (1993), bringing her signature combination of quirky charm and emotional vulnerability. The chemistry between Ryan and Kline elevates what could have been a standard romantic comedy into something more memorable.

The film's use of location shooting across France creates a vivid travelogue quality reminiscent of A Good Year (2006) and Under the Tuscan Sun (2003). The subplot involving wine culture and Kline's character's dream of owning a vineyard adds depth to what could have been a simple romance, much like how Sideways (2004) would later use wine country as both setting and metaphor. sections.content: French Kiss helped establish a specific romantic comedy subgenre that continues today with films like Midnight in Paris (2011) and Emily in Paris (2020). These films tap into American fantasies about French culture, romance, and lifestyle, often using the contrast between American pragmatism and French joie de vivre as a source of both comedy and character development.
